title: Dahlia
description: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family
wiki_lead:
Dahlia (UK:  DAY-lee-ə, US:  DA(H)L-yə, DAYL-yə) is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants native to Mexico and Central America. Dahlias are members of the Asteraceae (synonym name: Compositae) family of dicotyledonous plants, its relatives include the sunflower, daisy, chrysanthemum, and zinnia. There are 49 species of dahlia, with flowers in almost every hue (except blue), with hybrids commonly grown as garden plants.
Dahlias were known only to the Aztecs and other southern North American peoples until the Spanish conquest, after which the plants were brought to Europe. The tubers of some varieties are of medicinal and dietary value to humans because, in common with species of Inula and many other flowering plants, they use inulin, a polymer of the fruit sugar fructose, instead of starch as a storage polysaccharide.

Dahlia (UK:  DAY-lee-ə, US:  DA(H)L-yə, DAYL-yə) is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants native to Mexico and Central America. Dahlias are members of the Asteraceae (synonym name: Compositae) family of dicotyledonous plants, its relatives include the sunflower, daisy, chrysanthemum, and zinnia. There are 49 species of dahlia, with flowers in almost every hue (except blue), with hybrids commonly grown as garden plants.
Dahlias were known only to the Aztecs and other southern North American peoples until the Spanish conquest, after which the plants were brought to Europe. The tubers of some varieties are of medicinal and dietary value to humans because, in common with species of Inula and many other flowering plants, they use inulin, a polymer of the fruit sugar fructose, instead of starch as a storage polysaccharide.


Description

Dahlias are perennial plants with tuberous roots. They are not frost hardy, and require protection from frost if grown in regions with cold winters. While some have herbaceous stems, others have stems which lignify in the absence of secondary tissue and resprout following winter dormancy, allowing further seasons of growth.  As members of the family Asteraceae, dahlias have composite flower heads called capitula that are composed of multiple florets arranged in a central disc with surrounding petal-like rays. Each floret is a flower in its own right. The modern name Asteraceae comes from the type genus Aster and the Ancient Greek word for "star", referring to the appearance of a star with surrounding rays.
The stems are leafy, ranging in height from as low as 30 centimetres (12 inches) to more than 1.8–2.4 metres (6–8 feet). Flower forms are variable, with one head per stem; these can be as small as 5 cm (2 in) in diameter or up to 30 cm (1 ft) ("dinner plate"). The majority of species do not produce scented flowers. Like most plants that do not attract pollinating insects through scent, they are brightly colored, displaying most hues, with the exception of blue.
The great variety in species results from garden dahlias being octoploids, having eight sets of homologous chromosomes. In addition, dahlias also contain many transposons—genetic pieces that move from place to place upon an allele—which contributes to their manifesting such great diversity.

Early history

Spaniards reported finding the plants growing in Mexico in 1525, but the earliest known description is by Francisco Hernández, physician to Philip II, who was ordered to visit Mexico in 1570 to study the "natural products of that country". They were used as a source of food by the indigenous peoples, who both gathered wild specimens and cultivated crops. The indigenous peoples variously identified the plants as "Chichipatl" (Toltecs) and "Acocotle" or "Cocoxochitl" (Aztecs). From Hernández's perception of Nahuatl to Spanish (through various other translations) the word is "water cane", "water pipe", "water pipe flower", "hollow stem flower", or "cane flower", all referring to the hollow plant stems.
Hernandez described two varieties of dahlias (the pinwheel-like Dahlia pinnata and the huge Dahlia imperialis) as well as other medicinal plants of New Spain. Francisco Domínguez, an Hidalgo gentleman who accompanied Hernandez on part of his seven-year study, made a series of drawings to supplement the four volume report. Three of his drawings showed plants with flowers: two resembled the modern bedding dahlia, and one resembled the species Dahlia merckii; all displayed a high degree of doubleness. In 1578, a manuscript titled Nova Plantarum, Animalium et Mineralium Mexicanorum Historia, was sent back to the Escorial in Madrid. It was translated into Latin by Francisco Ximenes in 1615. In 1640, Francisco Cesi, President of the Academia dei Lincei of Rome, bought the Ximenes translation and, after annotating it, published it in 1649–1651 as two volumes, Rerum Medicarum Novae Hispaniae Thesaurus
grok_lead: Dahlia is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants in the Asteraceae (daisy) family, native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America, encompassing approximately 42 species. The genus name honors Anders Dahl, an 18th-century Swedish botanist. Dahlia is the national flower of Mexico, where species like D. pinnata were first discovered by Spanish explorers in the late 1700s and introduced to Europe around 1789. These plants are renowned for their showy, composite flowers, which feature a central disc surrounded by colorful ray florets in forms ranging from single and anemone-like to formal decorative and ball-shaped varieties. Heirloom varieties, primarily historical cultivars from the 19th and early 20th centuries, are particularly valued for their diverse flower forms, rich seasonal colors, and endurance. They exhibit a wide range of petal structures, including pompom types with tightly rolled, spiky, tubular petals; cactus types with elongated, pointed, often recurved or twisted petals; decorative types with broad, flat or slightly incurved petals; and others resembling daisies, anemones, or water lilies with more open or natural ray floret arrangements. Many heirloom dahlias feature less doubled blooms with visible centers and varied foliage. Blooms vary in size from 2 inches to over 12 inches in diameter and come in 15 official colors, including white, yellow, orange, pink, red, purple, and various blends, though true blue remains elusive. Over 50,000 cultivars have been developed worldwide through hybridization, primarily from species such as D. pinnata, D. coccinea, and D. variabilis, making dahlias a staple in ornamental gardening. Dahlias thrive in fertile, well-drained soil with full sun to partial shade and require regular watering, especially during dry spells, to produce abundant blooms from midsummer until the first frost. Grown from tubers, they reach heights of 1 to 6 feet depending on the cultivar and are typically treated as annuals in temperate climates, with tubers lifted and stored over winter in cooler zones. Beyond aesthetics, dahlias attract pollinators like bees and have historical uses in traditional medicine and as a food source for their edible tubers, rich in inulin. Their versatility in gardens, containers, and cut-flower arrangements underscores their enduring popularity among horticulturists.
